_note: AI-drafted Hausa A1 grammar lessons for Langi, not yet reviewed by a native speaker. Slugs match the ha catalog in lib/grammar.ts. Drill cues give the meaning, never the answer. Seeded by `npx tsx scripts/seed-grammar-ng.ts ha`. In examples, `fr` holds the Hausa sentence (field name kept from the original schema).

lessons.summary: Na, ka, ki, ya, ta, mun, kun and sun go before the verb to say what someone did.
lessons.explanation:
Hausa joins the subject and the tense into one small word before the verb. For a finished action (the completive) the forms are: na (I), ka (you, man), ki (you, woman), ya (he), ta (she), mun (we), kun (you, plural) and sun (they).

Na tafi gida means I went home. Ya ci abinci means he ate. Ta tafi kasuwa means she went to the market. Sun zo jiya means they came yesterday.

The verb itself stays the same, and the whole group sits right before it.

drills.prompt: ___ tafi kasuwa. (She went to the market)

lessons.summary: Ina, kana, kina, yana, tana, muna, kuna and suna plus a verbal noun mean is doing.
lessons.explanation:
For an action in progress, use these forms: ina (I am), kana (you, man, are), kina (you, woman, are), yana (he is), tana (she is), muna (we are), kuna (you, plural, are) and suna (they are).

After them comes a verbal noun, the form of the verb used for doing: Ina karatu (I am studying), Yana aiki (He is working), Tana girki (She is cooking), Suna wasa (They are playing), Muna cin abinci (We are eating).

The same pattern also says where someone is: Yana gida (He is at home).

lessons.summary: Zan, zaka, zaki, zai, za ta, za mu, za ku and za su mean will do.
lessons.explanation:
The future uses another set of pronoun forms: zan (I will), zaka (you, man), zaki (you, woman), zai (he), za ta (she), za mu (we), za ku (you, plural) and za su (they).

Zan tafi kasuwa gobe means I will go to the market tomorrow. Zai zo means he will come. Za mu ci abinci means we will eat. Za ta karanta littafi means she will read a book.

examples.en: I will go to the market tomorrow.

drills.prompt: Za ___ karanta littafi. (She will read a book)
Za su ___ Kano. (They will go to Kano)

lessons.summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine. Many nouns ending in -a are feminine, and the verb agrees: ya for masculine, ta for feminine.
lessons.explanation:
Hausa nouns are either masculine or feminine. A useful rule is that many nouns ending in -a are feminine: mota (car), yarinya (girl), kyanwa (cat). Others are masculine: yaro (boy), kare (dog), gida (house). Gida is an exception, since it ends in -a but is masculine, so learn the gender with each new noun.

The verb agrees with the noun: ya for a masculine subject, ta for a feminine one. Yaro ya tafi (The boy went), Yarinya ta tafi (The girl went), Mota ta lalace (The car broke down), Kyanwa ta yi barci (The cat slept).

lessons.summary: Ne and ce mean is after a noun: ne for masculine and plural, ce for feminine.
lessons.explanation:
To say what something is, put the noun first and add ne or ce after it. Use ne with a masculine noun (and with plurals) and ce with a feminine noun.

Shi malami ne (He is a teacher), Ita malama ce (She is a teacher), Wannan gida ne (This is a house), Wannan mota ce (This is a car). The same pattern works with ni (I): Ni dalibi ne (I am a student, a man).

To say where someone is, use the continuous forms with no ne or ce: Yana gida (He is at home), Tana kasuwa (She is at the market).

lessons.summary: Ba ... ba wraps the verb. Ban, bai, bata, basu and ba na mean did not and do not.
lessons.explanation:
A Hausa negative usually wraps the verb with ba before it and ba after it.

Past negative: ban (I did not), baka (you, man), baki (you, woman), bai (he), bata (she), bamu (we), baku (you, plural) and basu (they). Ban tafi ba (I did not go), Bai zo ba (He did not come), Bata ci abinci ba (She did not eat).

Present negative: ba na, ba ka, ba ki, ba ya, ba ta, ba mu, ba ku, ba su. Ba na ci nama (I do not eat meat), Ba ya aiki (He is not working).

drills.prompt: ___ ci abinci ba. (She did not eat)
Ba ___ ci nama. (I do not eat meat)

lessons.summary: Hausa plurals are irregular, so learn each pair: yaro to yara, mace to mata, gida to gidaje.
lessons.explanation:
Hausa has no single rule for making a plural, so learn each noun with its plural.

Common pairs: yaro, yara (boy, boys or children), mace, mata (woman, women), malami, malamai (teacher, teachers), littafi, littattafai (book, books) and gida, gidaje (house, houses).

A plural noun takes the same ne or ce pattern and plural pronouns: Su malamai ne (They are teachers).

lessons.summary: Add na after a masculine noun and ta after a feminine one for my: gidana (my house), motata (my car).
lessons.explanation:
Hausa attaches my, your and so on to the end of the noun. The ending depends on the noun's gender.

Masculine noun (gida, house): gidana (my), gidanka (your, man), gidanki (your, woman), gidansa (his), gidanta (her), gidanmu (our), gidanku (your, plural), gidansu (their).

Feminine noun (mota, car): motata (my), motarka (your, man), motarki (your, woman), motarsa (his), motarta (her), motarmu (our), motarku (your, plural), motarsu (their).
